title: Europe’s Geoeconomic Predicament
text:
← Back to Projects


Why is industrial policy en vogue in the European Union? The fear of falling behind has long driven European integration, but the answer used to be more market creation. Given the EU’s market-creating impetus, its tilt toward fiscal austerity, and its limits on state aid, there are many constraints to how industrial policy becomes part of the EU’s standard operating procedures.
My earlier work has traced the ideational and discursive politics behind key concepts such as open strategic autonomy and technological sovereignty, which have reoriented public policy from trade and industrial to digital policy. More recent work looked at how the EU’s flagship industrial policy tool - the important projects of common European interest - actually work on the ground. Ongoing work aims to examine the politics of Europe’s geoeconomic turn itself: why are firms not (or not equally) patriotic in how they support Europe’s quest for more autonomy over its economy?




Papers
Patriots or Profiteurs? (with R. Bosticco). Paper in progress. Explains how firms respond, economically and politically, to sovereignty-seeking policy in semiconductors and batteries.
The Costs of Conditionality (with T. Seidl and T. Wuttke). Competition & Change, 2026. Examines how the EU’s flagship industrial policy works on the ground.
Picking Losers (with T. Ergen). Regulation & Governance, 2025. Documents how decarbonization drew the EU into managing decline in targeted regions and sectors.
Moving On to Not Fall Behind? (with T. Seidl). Journal of European Public Policy, 2024. Reconstructs the “geo-dirigiste” turn through Europe’s fear of falling behind. JEPP Best Paper Prize 2024.
Europe First? (with D. Di Carlo). Journal of European Public Policy, 2023. Charts the rise of an EU industrial policy that promotes and protects the single market.
As Open as Possible, as Autonomous as Necessary (with T. Seidl). Journal of Common Market Studies, 2023. Shows how the Commission used open strategic autonomy as a coalition magnet.
When External Pressures Shift Domestic Coalitions (with J. Simons). Manuscript available upon request. Traces the Dutch shift from horizontal orthodoxy through covert verticalism to overt interventionism.
Whose Strategic Autonomy? (with D. Karas). Manuscript available upon request. Asks whether integration leaves Ukraine a raw-material supplier or moves it up the value chain.

title: Europe’s Geoeconomic Predicament
text:
The Challenge to Market-Based Governance
Why is industrial policy en vogue in the European Union? Given the EU’s market-making impetus, tilt towards fiscal austerity, and limits to subsidizing state aid, the turn to an active and targeted industrial policy in the last years is surprising. I argue that a declining belief in open markets and economic efficiency as the sole propagators of ‘good’ economic outcomes has mobilized a coalition of firms, business associations, and trade unions to challenge the EU’s market-based governance regime.

title: Europe’s Geoeconomic Predicament
text:
Manifestations
This is visible in EU trade policy, now understood in terms of open strategic autonomy, and especially visible in digital and high-tech fields and in the green transition, often discussed under the rubric of the ‘twin transitions’.

title: Luuk Schmitz
text:
Hello! I am a senior researcher at the Max Planck Institute for the Study of Societies (MPIfG) in Cologne. I hold a PhD in political and social science from the European University Institute with a dissertation on European industrial policy.
My research deals with the political economy of geoeconomics. I am interested in how multinational firms operate under geoeconomic tensions, how geoeconomics reshape trade and investment patterns, and how this affects decarbonization and the green transition. Geographically, I focus mostly on the European Union. Additionally, I have an interest in computational social science, and how we can bridge the gap between linguistics, computer science, and political science.
You can find more information about my research, publications, and contact info on this website. I occasionally post miscellaneous entries in my blog on more general academic interests.

title: Changing the Calculus on Economic Security
text:
← Back to Projects


Under globalization, firms built globe-spanning supply chains calibrated to deliver low lead times, efficiency, optimized to the last cent. That model presupposed geopolitical calm and legal certainty over property rights. Since the late 2010s, resurgent national industrial policy, tariffs, export controls, and war have thrown that model in disarray.
We are only beginning to understand how firms adapt their strategies, how this varies within and between sector, and how markets themselves are redrawn around new priorities. Moreover, a formidable challenge lies in how to measure changing corporate strategies: the firm as an organizing bureaucracy must be separated from the legal architecture - if not outright fiction - of the corporation.
This project’s aim is to provide a firm-level perspective on how geoeconomics are institutionalized in corporate strategy: from the way executives narrate their choices and analyses of the world to analysts in earnings calls, to what firms disclose in annual reports, and what they ultimately do to their ownership and supply chain structure.




Papers
The Geopolitical Construction of Markets. Manuscript available upon request. Traces how claims of necessity become durable participation in state projects.
Hierarchies of Adaptation. OSF Preprint, 2026. An earlier version of the argument.

title: Changing the Calculus on Economic Security
text:
Core Research Question
The core intuition behind the project is to place (real or imagined) security imperatives center stage. The aim of this project is to find out how such imperatives increasingly shape economic policy interventions, as well as corporate decision-making. We currently lack the theoretical and methodological toolkit to tackle such questions.
After several decades of intensifying globalization, the world has entered a new phase centered around geoeconomic fragmentation. Terms such as de-globalization, decoupling, and de-risking have entered public discourse and corporate reports, and increasingly shape policy interventions as governments vie to position themselves in a geopoliticizing world. An economic view centered around efficiency and factor endowment increasingly struggles to explain the security-based choices forced on firms and markets by states. From an efficiency-based point of view, replicating entire value chains within national borders is a form of economic downgrading. If so, why does this happen?

title: Changing the Calculus on Economic Security
text:
Methodology
The project goes beyond the usual ‘supply-side’ bias in the literature, which has so far mostly analyzed policy documents and individual companies. I have collected an original data set of corporate earnings calls (n=20.014) that involves more than 4500 companies and spans eight years (starting in 2016). The large number of firms allows for a large-scale and nuanced analysis of how geoeconomic competition affects firms and sectors across time.

title: Changing the Calculus on Economic Security
text:
Research Goals
In a first step, I aim to map theoretically and empirically what such an economic ‘calculus’ is, and how it is changing. In a follow-up paper, I want to analyze who are the winners and losers of geoeconomic competition.

title: Mesonomics: Rescaling Political Economy
text:
← Back to Projects


A major challenge for comparative and international political economists is the discrepancy between the behavior of statistical aggregates and that of individual agents. Our theories and methods of accounting remain separated between macro-institutional processes and micro-level outcomes in individual firms, organizations, and sectors. To assume away complexity by ignoring one or the other is to engage in what Thomas Oatley has called the reductionist gamble.
With the advent of economic statecraft and the weaponization of markets for geopolitical purposes comes an urgent need to understand how states and firms interact across markets, supply chains, and financial networks. The discovery of such meso-level processes has been labeled mesonomics.
The more widespread availability of firm-level data and the computational methods to analyze them now allows political economists to get more serious about addressing these questions. In my current work, firm-level data play a major role. Apart from the economic calculus project outlined above, I use data on the automobile industry to map the geographical dispersion and organization of car makers’ supply chains.




Resources
A Primer for the Use of Classifier and Generative Large Language Models in Social Science Research (with J. Cova). OSF Preprint, 2024. A practical guide, with replication materials.
The earnings-call and supply-chain database underpins Changing the Calculus on Economic Security and The Politics of Fracture.

title: Stacking Order
text:
← Back to Projects


What does global interdependence look like in a multipolar world? For decades, globalization has reshaped political rule, economic arrangements, social relationships, and cultural forms. A political order backed by American centrality in commerce, finance, technology, and defense fostered an economic order where markets opened, supply chains sprawled, and governance technocratized. The breakdown of this order coincides with a time of profound economic transformation. This book argues that the origin of this shift lies not in state strategy, but in changing corporate planning routines: the complexity and capital intensity of contemporary production (AI infrastructure, clean energy systems, semiconductor fabs) have outgrown the coordination capacity of price-driven markets. Firms have responded by vertically integrating supply chains, locking in standards, and building planning infrastructures that bundle physical resources, technical protocols, and industrial ecosystems into cohesive architectures of control. The walled gardens this creates serve equally well to increase profits as to enclose geopolitical space. As a consequence, geopolitical conflict tilts to which of these architectures national economies are wired into. Therefore, this book argues that the relevant political question in the 2020s isn’t market vs. state but rather which forms of non-market coordination prevail, who controls them, and whether democratic societies can govern them.

title: Corporate Planning and Grand Strategy
text:
← Back to Projects


Much like the 1930s and 1980s, geoeconomic conflict and great-power rivalry is synonymous with changing business models and new technologies. This project tries to unpack the green and digital transition as not just a conflict over regulating these technologies, but also about the underlying industrial organization. How amenable are electric cars and datacenters to globe-spanning, decentralized supply chains? The return of vertical integration in firms such as BYD, Amazon, and Meta would suggest that corporate organization itself changes with the technologies it builds its business around.
BYD produces an estimated 75 percent of its components in-house, designs its own silicon, and employs twice as many engineers as the Volkswagen group. Meanwhile, in the electronics supply chain, the rapid build-out of datacenters has led firms to enact a dense planning circuit where capacity and investment are synchronized and planned years into the future. In both cases, this dense corporate layer cake provides new levers for state power. Indeed, as these business models internationalize, they also raise questions over who controls the knowledge, equipment, and the capital needed to build a new generation of factories and what OpenAI now refers to as ‘compute campuses’.




Papers
Planning the Tech-Industrial Complex (with L. Dagorne). Under review. Shows how long-term contracts establish priority claims on future capacity, and why Washington underwrites them.
Vertical Integration in the Electric Vehicle Revolution (with P. Gerbaudo and G. Anzolin). Manuscript available upon request. Compares BYD and Tesla with Toyota and Volkswagen.
What Is Different About Chinese Automotive Capitalism? (with P. Polyak). Paper in progress. Shows how integration, demand pressures, and geopolitical steering combine to carry industrial stacks abroad.

title: The Politics of Fracture
text:
← Back to Projects


In 2018, the electrical-equipment maker Eaton filed more than sixty individual requests to be exempted from American steel tariffs. Three years later, it lobbied for clean-energy credits through a lobbying firm shared with a power producer, an offshore-wind developer, and a biofuels company. Theories of trade politics struggle to explain such political behavior. They see value chains as the scaffolding of coaltions. This project argues that under geoeconomics, they now become sites of fracture or smaller, program-specific coalitions. For firms, geoeconomics ultimately means one of three things: a price or restriction to access partners or markets, an inducement to state-defined behavior, or a shock that changes the firm’s market position.
The project traces what becomes of business politics when geoeconomics arrive through these three channels. Restrictions offer relief that each firm claims for itself. What is more, firms down the chain can object to each others relief. Inducements create programs that must be won and defended together by beneficiaries that are defined by the program’s incentives (e.g., IRA tax credits). Shocks such as the Ukraine war or the Strait of Hormuz don’t have a political instrument behind them. They create transitory winners and losers (think for instance of shipping firms adding tonne mileage when a route closes down).
The upshot of the project is to see how geoeconomics changes from a buzzword to something that political scientists can analyze: changing the venue (the executive) and the substance (coalitions, firms) of where distributive conflict play out.




Papers
Exit, Coalitions, and Anomy: Business Politics under Geoeconomics. Paper in progress. Links exposure in earnings calls to federal lobbying disclosures, tariff-relief petitions, and firm-to-firm supply-chain networks.
